title: Clarifying Requirements
summary: The questions worth asking in the first five minutes of a system design interview, and the ones that just burn the interviewer's patience.

slides.markdown:
Every system design interview opens the same way whether the interviewer says it or not: figure out what you're actually building before you build it. That means separating **functional requirements** (what the system must do) from **non-functional requirements** (how well it must do it), and deciding what's explicitly out of scope.

Done well, this takes under five minutes and shapes every decision after it. Done badly — either skipped or dragged out — it's the [interview framework's](the-interview-framework) most common failure point.

slides.sectionTitle: Functional requirements: what must the system do, precisely
slides.markdown:
**Functional requirements** are the concrete actions the system supports — post a tweet, follow a user, search a listing, process a payment. Vague functional requirements produce vague designs, so the goal is to make them specific enough to design against.

For "design Twitter," "users can post content" is too loose — does that include images and video, or text only? Can a post be edited after publishing? Is there a character limit? Each answer changes the storage model and the write path.

Ask until you could describe each feature as a one-line API call — `postTweet(userId, text)` — not just a feature name.

slides.sectionTitle: Non-functional requirements: scale, latency, availability, consistency
slides.markdown:
**Non-functional requirements** describe quality, not features: how many users, how fast must a read return, what happens during a network partition, can two users briefly see different data. These numbers decide the architecture far more than the feature list does.

A feed that must load in under 200ms for 50 million daily users needs precomputed, cached results; the same feed at 50,000 users can query on demand. A payment system that can never show stale balances needs strong consistency; a like-counter tolerating a few seconds of lag can use an eventually-consistent counter.

Always ask for a rough number, even a guess — "is this more like a thousand or a million users?" — rather than designing against "a lot."

![Each requirement question mapped to the design decision it drives](assets/requirements-decision-map.svg)

Each requirement question exists because it forecloses or unlocks a specific design decision downstream — it isn't a box-ticking ritual. A latency target rules certain databases out; a consistency requirement rules certain replication strategies out.

If you can't name which later decision a question would affect, it's probably not worth asking.

slides.sectionTitle: Scoping down: what to explicitly exclude and say out loud
slides.markdown:
A 45-minute interview cannot cover everything a real system like Twitter or Uber does — deliberately narrowing scope is expected, not a shortcut you're getting away with. The mistake is narrowing it silently and hoping nobody notices.

Say the exclusion out loud: "I'll focus on posting and reading the home timeline, and set aside direct messages and ads for now — let me know if you want those included." This does two things: it protects you from being asked about something you haven't designed for, and it gives the interviewer a chance to redirect if that excluded piece is actually the point of the question.

Scoping down is a sign of judgment; scoping down without saying so is a gap waiting to be found.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: good questions vs questions that stall the interview
slides.markdown:
Not all clarifying questions earn their keep. The good ones change a design decision; the stalling ones just consume the clock.

| | Good question | Stalling question |
|---|---|---|
| Example | "Roughly how many daily active users?" | "What programming language should I use?" |
| Changes | Storage, caching, sharding strategy | Nothing about the architecture |
| Interviewer reads it as | Scoping the problem | Avoiding the problem |
| When to ask | Before any design decision that depends on it | Rarely relevant to a system design round |

**How to decide:** before asking, silently finish the sentence "the answer would change my design by..." — if you can't fill it in, skip the question.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: asking so many questions the interviewer runs out of patience
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The more questions I ask, the more thorough I look."

**Why it's wrong:** past a certain point, extra questions stop signaling rigor and start signaling stalling or indecision — especially questions whose answer wouldn't actually change anything about the design. An interviewer who's answered eight questions in six minutes starts wondering if you know how to start.

**Correct model:** ask a tight, high-value set — functional scope, rough scale, latency/consistency needs, and one or two exclusions — then state your assumptions for anything smaller and move on. "I'll assume a typical social app's read-heavy pattern unless you tell me otherwise" keeps momentum without sacrificing rigor.
